raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to address an attractive but unproven premise: that temporary coronary scaffolding could provide acute lumen gain and drug delivery, then disappear, restoring vasomotion, adaptive remodelling, and future surgical or percutaneous options. The concept predates contemporary drug-eluting stents (DES). The Igaki–Tamai poly-L-lactic acid scaffold showed feasibility but required bulky struts and thermal balloon expansion [1]. Long-term follow-up suggested acceptable late safety, yet also highlighted that proof of biological plausibility is not the same as superiority over metallic DES [2]. Magnesium scaffolds offered a different resorption pathway and better early deliverability, but the first PROGRESS-AMS device lost radial strength rapidly, producing high restenosis [3].

The most influential coronary BVS was the everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold. Early first-in-human and imaging studies generated enthusiasm by showing acceptable acute success, late lumen preservation in selected lesions, and evidence of strut coverage and resorption [4], [5]. These observations stimulated a broader mechanistic narrative: after polymer degradation, the treated segment might recover endothelial function, cyclic strain, and expansive remodelling, reducing very late events that had been observed with permanent implants [6]. However, early studies enrolled simple lesions, used intensive imaging, and were not powered for uncommon safety endpoints.

Randomised trials changed the field. ABSORB II showed similar early clinical outcomes but did not demonstrate the expected vasomotor advantage, and three-year follow-up showed higher target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis with Absorb compared with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents [7], [8]. ABSORB III, conducted for regulatory approval, met non-inferiority for target-lesion failure at one year in relatively simple lesions, but numerically higher device thrombosis foreshadowed later concerns [9]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China broadly confirmed procedural feasibility, yet did not remove uncertainty about safety margins when compared with best-in-class DES [10], [11]. The AIDA all-comers trial was pivotal: routine BVS use was associated with significantly higher definite or probable device thrombosis, prompting early reporting and practice change [12]. ABSORB IV incorporated more stringent implantation technique and excluded very small vessels, improving early performance but not establishing an advantage over metallic DES [13]. Longer-term ABSORB III follow-up suggested that excess risk was concentrated before complete bioresorption, but a durable clinical benefit after resorption remained difficult to prove [14].

Meta-analyses reinforced these findings. Randomised evidence consistently demonstrated higher scaffold thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction with first-generation Absorb compared with metallic everolimus-eluting stents [15], [16]. Network and aggregate analyses reached similar conclusions: any theoretical late benefit was outweighed, at least during the first three years, by early and late thrombotic hazard [17]. Mechanistic studies identified several contributors, including thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, malapposition, underdeployment, scaffold discontinuity during resorption, and implantation in small vessels [18]. Intravascular imaging of very late scaffold thrombosis showed patterns such as uncovered or malapposed struts, dismantling, neoatherosclerosis, and peri-strut low-intensity areas [19], [20]. Registry experience, including GHOST-EU, confirmed that real-world outcomes were more adverse than early feasibility studies suggested [21], [22].

Technique became central. The “PSP” approach—adequate lesion preparation, accurate vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—was associated with fewer adverse events, especially when very small vessels were avoided [23]. Nevertheless, the need for meticulous technique exposed a key limitation: a device intended for broad PCI use had less procedural forgiveness than contemporary DES, whose thin struts, deliverability, and safety had improved substantially during the same period. Prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy was often advocated after BVS implantation, particularly during the resorption window, but this reduced one of the hoped-for practical advantages.

Non-polymeric and next-generation scaffolds remain scientifically important. The drug-eluting absorbable magnesium scaffold programme showed improved radial strength and restenosis compared with bare magnesium predecessors [24], with encouraging mid-term outcomes in selected lesions [25]. Earlier DREAMS experience helped establish magnesium as a plausible platform [26]. Other polymeric devices, including DESolve, Fantom, and MeRes100, attempted to improve strut thickness, expansion behaviour, radiopacity, and degradation kinetics [27], [28], [29]. Yet none has displaced contemporary metallic DES, and the evidentiary bar is now higher: new scaffolds must show not merely feasibility, but non-inferior safety with a credible late clinical advantage.

At present, BVS should be viewed as a cautionary innovation in PCI. The biological rationale remains compelling, but first-generation clinical experience showed that resorption alone does not guarantee better outcomes. Future success likely requires thinner struts, predictable radial strength, benign degradation, excellent radiopacity, broad overexpansion capacity, simplified implantation, and adequately powered trials extending beyond complete resorption [30]. Until such evidence exists, contemporary thin-strut metallic DES remain the standard for most PCI, while BVS occupy a research-oriented role in carefully selected patients and lesions.
